# Taking the planner to other festivals — a first design sketch

> **Status: rudimentary.** This is a sketch, not a plan of record. Nothing here
> is committed to, no code change is proposed yet, and several sections end in a
> question rather than an answer. Its job is to make the shape of the problem
> visible — and in particular to surface the Edinburgh assumptions that are
> currently invisible because they are spelled as constants, comments and
> regexes rather than as configuration.
>
> Scope: the **planner** (`/plan`) primarily, since that is where the model
> lives; the Now page is noted where it differs.

---

## 1. What the planning model actually is

Stripped of Edinburgh, the planner is four pure computations over a catalogue of
`{show → performances[]}` with venue coordinates:

| Step | Module | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| favourites text → show IDs | `plan/lib/favourites.js` | a stable show ID and a canonical show URL |
| performances → *available* performances | `plan/lib/availability.js` | a ticket-status vocabulary |
| venue pair → travel minutes | `plan/lib/travel.js` | coordinates + a speed model |
| available performances → clash-free itinerary | `plan/lib/engine.js` | a day window, meal bands, per-day caps |
| itinerary → CSV / ICS | `plan/lib/itinerary.js` | a timezone and a wall-clock convention |

**None of that is Edinburgh-specific in principle.** "Given a set of things I
want to see, each with several showings across a date range, in venues that take
time to travel between — which can I actually fit?" is a general problem. The
earliest-finish-first greedy in `engine.js` does not know what a Fringe is.

What *is* Edinburgh-specific is everything around it: where the catalogue comes
from, what its ticket statuses are called, what a date window looks like, what
currency and language it is in, and how a user's shortlist gets into the tool.
Those are the four sections below.

---

## 2. Data accessibility — the binding constraint

This decides feasibility, and it is worse than the language problem.

### 2.1 The tiers

Any candidate festival falls into one of four tiers, and the tier — not the
festival's size — determines the cost:

- **Tier 1 — official, licensed API.** A documented feed with an access key.
  Cheap, legally clean, and stable across years.
- **Tier 2 — an undocumented but stable web API.** What edfringe.com actually
  is today: a Next.js SPA over a Tikketr GraphQL endpoint, reachable with public
  anonymous credentials (see [`scraper/SCRAPING.md`](../scraper/SCRAPING.md)).
  Workable, but it breaks without notice and carries no licence.
- **Tier 3 — HTML scraping only.** Per-festival parsers, brittle against every
  site redesign, and a per-festival maintenance burden that compounds.
- **Tier 4 — no machine-readable programme.** A PDF brochure and a paper guide.
  Not viable.

### 2.2 What we know today

Edinburgh is unusually well served, and this is easy to mistake for normal:

- **Tier 2 is already built** — the Tikketr GraphQL scrape in `scraper/`.
- **Tier 1 exists and is not currently used.** The
  [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)
  is a free API over the official listings database for *all eleven* Edinburgh
  festivals (640,000+ performances), with `events` and `venues` endpoints and a
  self-service access key.

That second point deserves a decision of its own, because whichever source is
chosen becomes the template every other city is fitted to. Its terms are not
free of consequences for this repo's architecture:

- Fringe listings require **separate approval from a Fringe review team**;
  development happens against a demonstration dataset first.
- Applications must **refresh at least every 24 hours**, and must **not
  redistribute the data as a static dump to third parties**.
- Show links must **deep-link to edfringe.com**, and the app must state it is not
  official.

This repo currently commits generated `data/` files to git and serves them from
GitHub Pages — which is, read strictly, a static dump published to the world on
a scrape cadence rather than a 24-hour client refresh. Whether that is compatible
with the licence is an open legal/architectural question, and it is a *prerequisite*
for the multi-festival work rather than a detail of it, because the answer
("client fetches a live feed" vs. "we ship a snapshot") changes the whole data
layer.

For every other candidate city, no equivalent Tier 1 source has been found.
Assume Tier 2 or Tier 3 per festival until a probe says otherwise.

### 2.3 The favourites-import problem is per-festival

The planner's front door — a shortlist you already built elsewhere — is the least
portable part of the product. Today it depends on:

- `plan/lib/favourites.js:7` — a regex hard-coded to
  `edfringe.com/tickets/whats-on/<slug>`;
- the fact that edfringe.com has favouriting at all;
- a **third-party Chrome extension** to get that list out as CSV, since no native
  export is documented.

That chain has to be re-established, festival by festival, and there is no reason
to expect it exists. A portable product probably cannot depend on it: the
in-tool search path (`plan/lib/search.js`, already built) is the one intake that
travels, and for a new festival it may have to be the *only* one.

---

## 3. Integration — what the code would need

### 3.1 A festival descriptor

The natural shape is one **festival adapter** plus one **festival descriptor**,
with the pure engine untouched. The descriptor is the config object that every
constant listed in §5 currently stands in for:

```
{
  id, name,
  city, country,
  locale, timezone, currency,
  runStart, runEnd,              // real dates, not "August 1–31"
  siteBase, showUrlPattern,      // deep-link contract
  imageHostPrefix,
  ticketStatus: { unavailable[], nonTicketed[] },
  genres[], subgenres[],         // per-festival taxonomy, not a shared enum
  travel: { modes[], speedsKmh{} },
  defaultCentre: [lat, lng],
  geocodeBounds,
}
```

Two design calls worth making early, because they are hard to reverse:

- **One descriptor per *festival*, not per *city*.** Edinburgh in August is six
  festivals with different date ranges and different data sources. If the unit is
  a city, the Adelaide/Avignon cases fit but Edinburgh itself does not.
- **Taxonomies are per-festival data, not a shared enum.** edfringe's 10 genres
  and 104 subgenres are its own vocabulary. Mapping Avignon's *théâtre / humour /
  cirque* split onto it would be a lossy translation nobody asked for. A shared
  cross-festival taxonomy is a much later problem, and probably not worth it.

### 3.2 The adapter boundary

`scraper/` becomes per-festival fetchers behind one normalizer contract, rather
than one script that knows edfringe's schema. The contract is already implicitly
defined — `data/normalized/shows.json`'s shape, decoded by `js/app.js`'s
`adaptShow` and `plan/lib/hydrate.js`'s `rehydrateShows` — but it is not written
down anywhere as a spec, and it uses **positional index encoding** against
`data/venues.json`'s global lookup lists. Any second festival forces that
implicit contract to become explicit, and the positional encoding to become
per-festival rather than global.

### 3.3 Data layout and payload

Today the planner fetches the full `data/normalized/shows.json` (~1.1 MB gzipped,
4,078 shows) on load. That is already noted as borderline in
[`plan/README.md`](../plan/README.md). Multi-festival makes it a real constraint,
and the fix is structural rather than an optimisation: data is partitioned per
festival (`data/<festival-id>/…`) and only the selected festival's file is
fetched. Which festival is selected has to come from the URL — `/plan/` becomes
`/<festival>/plan/` or `/plan/?f=<festival>` — so that a shared link opens the
right catalogue.

### 3.4 What stays untouched

`plan/lib/engine.js` should not change at all. If a festival adapter requires an
engine change, that is a signal the descriptor is missing a field.

---

## 4. Localization and translation

Four separable problems, routinely conflated:

**a. UI strings.** There is no i18n layer at all today — every label is a literal
in `plan/plan.js`, `js/app.js` and the two `index.html` files, both of which are
`<html lang="en">`. Introducing one is mechanical but touches everything, and
should happen before, not after, a second locale exists.

**b. Content strings — the hard one.** Show titles, descriptions, company names,
venue names and content warnings come from the festival, in the festival's
language. Avignon OFF is ~90% French companies; there is no English corpus to
serve. This means:

- a localized UI over French content is the *realistic* target, not a fully
  translated product;
- machine-translating descriptions is possible but is a per-show cost against
  1,780 shows and a quality risk on marketing copy;
- **search must work in the content's language.** `plan/lib/search.js` matching
  needs diacritic-insensitive normalization (`théâtre` ≈ `theatre`) and
  locale-aware collation before it is useful in French, and the same again for
  Romanian (Sibiu) or Italian (Milan).

**c. Formatting and units.** Dates (`js/app.js:2544` hard-codes `en-GB`),
24-hour vs. 12-hour clocks (Adelaide and Charleston are 12-hour cultures; the
planner's axis is 24-hour and runs to `27:00`), first day of week (the "best
Sat–Sun weekend" heuristic is not universal), and currency — `£` appears as a
literal in `plan/index.html:298`, `plan/plan.js:1588` and the `search.js` price
contract. `Intl.NumberFormat` and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` cover most of this once
a locale exists to pass them.

**d. Timezone.** `plan/lib/itinerary.js:141` hard-codes `TZID = "Europe/London"`
for ICS export. This is currently *correct and deliberate* — floating local time
is right for an on-the-ground plan — but it must become a descriptor field.
Adelaide adds a genuinely awkward case: `Australia/Adelaide` is UTC+9:30, and the
Fringe run (20 Feb – 22 Mar) **crosses a daylight-saving transition**, so a
naive wall-clock model drifts by an hour mid-festival.

**Sequencing note:** (a) and (c) are prerequisites for any non-UK festival —
including English-speaking Adelaide and Perth. (b) is what makes Avignon
expensive. So the cheapest second market is Brighton or Perth, not the closest
structural twin.

---

## 5. Edinburgh-specific assumptions currently baked in

These are the "aspects not considered" — the places where Edinburgh is spelled as
a constant rather than as config. Grouped by how hard they are to unpick.

### Hard — model-level, not just a constant

- **The calendar axis is one calendar month.** `plan/plan.js:56-59` fixes
  `YEAR = 2026`, `MONTH = "08"`, `DAYS_IN_MONTH = 31`, `FEST_START_DAY = 7`, and
  the whole grid, date-window scrubber and "pick my best dates" search iterate
  over days 1–31 of that month. **Adelaide Fringe runs 20 Feb – 22 Mar** — the
  second-largest fringe in the world breaks this on day one. Piccolo Spoleto
  (22 May – 7 Jun) and Perth (Jan–Feb) break it too. The axis has to become an
  arbitrary date range, which is a rewrite of the calendar rendering and the
  window maths, not a config swap.
- **The day axis is 09:00 → 27:00** (`plan/plan.js:70-71`), with a default day end
  of 25:00, because a Fringe evening runs past midnight and late shows fold onto
  the previous festival night. That is a real cultural property of *this*
  festival. A design-week or exhibition festival is a 10:00–18:00 opening-hours
  model with no after-midnight concept at all, and a Spanish-scheduled festival
  would push later still.
- **Every show has ticketed performances with start times.** Milan's Fuorisalone,
  the Edinburgh Art Festival and the Venice Biennale are *exhibitions* — open
  during hours, not at times. The scheduling engine has no concept of "drop in
  any time between 10:00 and 18:00, allow 45 minutes", and that is arguably the
  single largest missing capability for the non-theatre candidates.
- **Ticket-status vocabulary is Tikketr's enum.** `plan/lib/availability.js:22`
  denylists `SOLD_OUT`, `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` and friends — values from
  one ticketing platform. Another festival's platform has a different vocabulary,
  or none. The concept ("is this bookable") generalises; the strings do not.
- **The show ID is an edfringe slug.** It is the join key between favourites,
  the catalogue and deep links (`plan/lib/favourites.js:7,28`). Portability needs
  a `(festivalId, showId)` pair throughout, including in `localStorage` keys —
  otherwise a stored Edinburgh shortlist collides with an Adelaide one.

### Medium — tuned values presented as physics

- **Walking speed is Edinburgh's terrain.** `plan/lib/travel.js:18` dials walking
  down to ~3.33 km/h explicitly because of "Edinburgh's closes, hills, stairs and
  festival crowds", and `car: 22` km/h is calibrated to "the congested August city
  centre". Applied to flat, sprawling Adelaide these are simply wrong — and wrong
  in the direction that silently drops schedulable shows.
- **There is no public-transport mode.** `plan/lib/travel.js:12` offers walk/bike/
  car only, with the stated reason that honest headway-aware bus times aren't
  available. That is defensible in a compact walkable centre. In Adelaide (562
  venues), Melbourne or Montreal, transit *is* the mode, and its absence is a
  correctness problem rather than a missing nicety.
- **Crow-flies distance stands in for routing.** Fine across Edinburgh's Old Town;
  much worse across a river, a rail corridor or Venice's canals.
- **Geography defaults.** `js/app.js:20` defaults to central Edinburgh;
  `js/places.js:17,30` bounds the Nominatim geocoder to a greater-Edinburgh box
  and `inEdinburgh()` gates results by it; `shared/geo.js:12` deliberately ignores
  a real user location that is nowhere near Edinburgh. All three are correct today
  and all three actively break elsewhere.

### Easy — one-line config once a descriptor exists

- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:141` — `TZID = "Europe/London"` (but see the DST note in §4d).
- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:197` — ICS UIDs suffixed `@edfringenow.com`.
- `plan/lib/hydrate.js:13` — `IMAGE_HOST_PREFIX` pinned to `registration.edfringe.com`.
- `js/app.js:2544` — `en-GB` date formatting.
- `plan/index.html:298`, `plan/plan.js:1588`, `plan/lib/search.js:12,50` — `£`.
- `shared/affiliates.js:75` — Booking.com search hard-coded to `ss: "Edinburgh"`,
  and the Omio route pages likewise. Affiliate partners and their coverage differ
  by country, so this is easy to *parameterise* and separately a commercial
  question.

### Product-level, outside the code

- **The brand is the city.** "EdFringeNow", `edfringenow.com`, and the ICS UID
  domain all name one festival. A multi-festival product needs a different name,
  and that decision gates the domain and the deep-link contract.
- **"Two or three shows a day" and "don't fill the day"** are Fringe-culture
  advice this product's defaults encode. They may not be the right defaults for a
  design week or a jazz festival.

---

## 6. A plausible order of work

Sequenced so each step is useful on its own and none is wasted if the next is
never taken:

1. **Resolve the data-source question for Edinburgh itself** (Tier 1 official API
   vs. the current Tier 2 scrape, and whether committed static data is licence-
   compatible). This sets the pattern for everything after it.
2. **Make the calendar an arbitrary date range** instead of a fixed month. This is
   independently correct — the current data already spans 24 Jul – 31 Aug and the
   July previews fall off the axis — and it is the largest single blocker.
3. **Extract the festival descriptor** and route the constants in §5 through it,
   with Edinburgh as the only entry. No behaviour change; the diff is the point.
4. **Add an i18n layer and `Intl`-based formatting**, still English-only.
5. **Prove it with a second English festival** (Brighton or Perth) end to end,
   including the intake question — that is where the model gets tested, not the
   engine.
6. Only then consider a non-English festival, and only with the translation cost
   in §4b priced honestly.

---

## 7. What this sketch does not answer

- Whether any candidate festival has an accessible programme at all. Every
  feasibility claim above is conditional on a probe nobody has run.
- Whether the Edinburgh Festivals Listings API licence permits this repo's
  committed-static-data architecture. §2.2 raises it; it is unresolved.
- How exhibition-style events (open hours, no start times) would be modelled — the
  gap that rules out most of the non-theatre candidates as things stand.
- Whether a second festival is a second *market* or a second *product*. If the
  audiences don't overlap, most of the leverage assumed here doesn't exist.
- Anything about cost, demand or commercial viability. This is a technical sketch
  only.

## 1. What the planning model actually is

Stripped of Edinburgh, the planner is four pure computations over a catalogue of
`{show → performances[]}` with venue coordinates:

| Step | Module | Depends on |
|---|---|---|
| favourites text → show IDs | `plan/lib/favourites.js` | a stable show ID and a canonical show URL |
| performances → *available* performances | `plan/lib/availability.js` | a ticket-status vocabulary |
| venue pair → travel minutes | `plan/lib/travel.js` | coordinates + a speed model |
| available performances → clash-free itinerary | `plan/lib/engine.js` | a day window, meal bands, per-day caps |
| itinerary → CSV / ICS | `plan/lib/itinerary.js` | a timezone and a wall-clock convention |

**None of that is Edinburgh-specific in principle.** "Given a set of things I
want to see, each with several showings across a date range, in venues that take
time to travel between — which can I actually fit?" is a general problem. The
earliest-finish-first greedy in `engine.js` does not know what a Fringe is.

What *is* Edinburgh-specific is everything around it: where the catalogue comes
from, what its ticket statuses are called, what a date window looks like, what
currency and language it is in, and how a user's shortlist gets into the tool.
Those are the four sections below.

---

## 2. Data accessibility — the binding constraint

This decides feasibility, and it is worse than the language problem.

### 2.1 The tiers

Any candidate festival falls into one of four tiers, and the tier — not the
festival's size — determines the cost:

- **Tier 1 — official, licensed API.** A documented feed with an access key.
  Cheap, legally clean, and stable across years.
- **Tier 2 — an undocumented but stable web API.** What edfringe.com actually
  is today: a Next.js SPA over a Tikketr GraphQL endpoint, reachable with public
  anonymous credentials (see [`scraper/SCRAPING.md`](../scraper/SCRAPING.md)).
  Workable, but it breaks without notice and carries no licence.
- **Tier 3 — HTML scraping only.** Per-festival parsers, brittle against every
  site redesign, and a per-festival maintenance burden that compounds.
- **Tier 4 — no machine-readable programme.** A PDF brochure and a paper guide.
  Not viable.

### 2.2 What we know today

Edinburgh is unusually well served, and this is easy to mistake for normal:

- **Tier 2 is already built** — the Tikketr GraphQL scrape in `scraper/`.
- **Tier 1 exists and is not currently used.** The
  [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)
  is a free API over the official listings database for *all eleven* Edinburgh
  festivals (640,000+ performances), with `events` and `venues` endpoints and a
  self-service access key.

That second point deserves a decision of its own, because whichever source is
chosen becomes the template every other city is fitted to. Its terms are not
free of consequences for this repo's architecture:

- Fringe listings require **separate approval from a Fringe review team**;
  development happens against a demonstration dataset first.
- Applications must **refresh at least every 24 hours**, and must **not
  redistribute the data as a static dump to third parties**.
- Show links must **deep-link to edfringe.com**, and the app must state it is not
  official.

This repo currently commits generated `data/` files to git and serves them from
GitHub Pages — which is, read strictly, a static dump published to the world on
a scrape cadence rather than a 24-hour client refresh. Whether that is compatible
with the licence is an open legal/architectural question, and it is a *prerequisite*
for the multi-festival work rather than a detail of it, because the answer
("client fetches a live feed" vs. "we ship a snapshot") changes the whole data
layer.

For every other candidate city, no equivalent Tier 1 source has been found.
Assume Tier 2 or Tier 3 per festival until a probe says otherwise.

### 2.3 The favourites-import problem is per-festival

The planner's front door — a shortlist you already built elsewhere — is the least
portable part of the product. Today it depends on:

- `plan/lib/favourites.js:7` — a regex hard-coded to
  `edfringe.com/tickets/whats-on/<slug>`;
- the fact that edfringe.com has favouriting at all;
- a **third-party Chrome extension** to get that list out as CSV, since no native
  export is documented.

That chain has to be re-established, festival by festival, and there is no reason
to expect it exists. A portable product probably cannot depend on it: the
in-tool search path (`plan/lib/search.js`, already built) is the one intake that
travels, and for a new festival it may have to be the *only* one.

---

## 3. Integration — what the code would need

### 3.1 A festival descriptor

The natural shape is one **festival adapter** plus one **festival descriptor**,
with the pure engine untouched. The descriptor is the config object that every
constant listed in §5 currently stands in for:

```
{
  id, name,
  city, country,
  locale, timezone, currency,
  runStart, runEnd,              // real dates, not "August 1–31"
  siteBase, showUrlPattern,      // deep-link contract
  imageHostPrefix,
  ticketStatus: { unavailable[], nonTicketed[] },
  genres[], subgenres[],         // per-festival taxonomy, not a shared enum
  travel: { modes[], speedsKmh{} },
  defaultCentre: [lat, lng],
  geocodeBounds,
}
```

Two design calls worth making early, because they are hard to reverse:

- **One descriptor per *festival*, not per *city*.** Edinburgh in August is six
  festivals with different date ranges and different data sources. If the unit is
  a city, the Adelaide/Avignon cases fit but Edinburgh itself does not.
- **Taxonomies are per-festival data, not a shared enum.** edfringe's 10 genres
  and 104 subgenres are its own vocabulary. Mapping Avignon's *théâtre / humour /
  cirque* split onto it would be a lossy translation nobody asked for. A shared
  cross-festival taxonomy is a much later problem, and probably not worth it.

### 3.2 The adapter boundary

`scraper/` becomes per-festival fetchers behind one normalizer contract, rather
than one script that knows edfringe's schema. The contract is already implicitly
defined — `data/normalized/shows.json`'s shape, decoded by `js/app.js`'s
`adaptShow` and `plan/lib/hydrate.js`'s `rehydrateShows` — but it is not written
down anywhere as a spec, and it uses **positional index encoding** against
`data/venues.json`'s global lookup lists. Any second festival forces that
implicit contract to become explicit, and the positional encoding to become
per-festival rather than global.

### 3.3 Data layout and payload

Today the planner fetches the full `data/normalized/shows.json` (~1.1 MB gzipped,
4,078 shows) on load. That is already noted as borderline in
[`plan/README.md`](../plan/README.md). Multi-festival makes it a real constraint,
and the fix is structural rather than an optimisation: data is partitioned per
festival (`data/<festival-id>/…`) and only the selected festival's file is
fetched. Which festival is selected has to come from the URL — `/plan/` becomes
`/<festival>/plan/` or `/plan/?f=<festival>` — so that a shared link opens the
right catalogue.

### 3.4 What stays untouched

`plan/lib/engine.js` should not change at all. If a festival adapter requires an
engine change, that is a signal the descriptor is missing a field.

---

## 4. Localization and translation

Four separable problems, routinely conflated:

**a. UI strings.** There is no i18n layer at all today — every label is a literal
in `plan/plan.js`, `js/app.js` and the two `index.html` files, both of which are
`<html lang="en">`. Introducing one is mechanical but touches everything, and
should happen before, not after, a second locale exists.

**b. Content strings — the hard one.** Show titles, descriptions, company names,
venue names and content warnings come from the festival, in the festival's
language. Avignon OFF is ~90% French companies; there is no English corpus to
serve. This means:

- a localized UI over French content is the *realistic* target, not a fully
  translated product;
- machine-translating descriptions is possible but is a per-show cost against
  1,780 shows and a quality risk on marketing copy;
- **search must work in the content's language.** `plan/lib/search.js` matching
  needs diacritic-insensitive normalization (`théâtre` ≈ `theatre`) and
  locale-aware collation before it is useful in French, and the same again for
  Romanian (Sibiu) or Italian (Milan).

**c. Formatting and units.** Dates (`js/app.js:2544` hard-codes `en-GB`),
24-hour vs. 12-hour clocks (Adelaide and Charleston are 12-hour cultures; the
planner's axis is 24-hour and runs to `27:00`), first day of week (the "best
Sat–Sun weekend" heuristic is not universal), and currency — `£` appears as a
literal in `plan/index.html:298`, `plan/plan.js:1588` and the `search.js` price
contract. `Intl.NumberFormat` and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` cover most of this once
a locale exists to pass them.

**d. Timezone.** `plan/lib/itinerary.js:141` hard-codes `TZID = "Europe/London"`
for ICS export. This is currently *correct and deliberate* — floating local time
is right for an on-the-ground plan — but it must become a descriptor field.
Adelaide adds a genuinely awkward case: `Australia/Adelaide` is UTC+9:30, and the
Fringe run (20 Feb – 22 Mar) **crosses a daylight-saving transition**, so a
naive wall-clock model drifts by an hour mid-festival.

**Sequencing note:** (a) and (c) are prerequisites for any non-UK festival —
including English-speaking Adelaide and Perth. (b) is what makes Avignon
expensive. So the cheapest second market is Brighton or Perth, not the closest
structural twin.

---

## 5. Edinburgh-specific assumptions currently baked in

These are the "aspects not considered" — the places where Edinburgh is spelled as
a constant rather than as config. Grouped by how hard they are to unpick.

### Hard — model-level, not just a constant

- **The calendar axis is one calendar month.** `plan/plan.js:56-59` fixes
  `YEAR = 2026`, `MONTH = "08"`, `DAYS_IN_MONTH = 31`, `FEST_START_DAY = 7`, and
  the whole grid, date-window scrubber and "pick my best dates" search iterate
  over days 1–31 of that month. **Adelaide Fringe runs 20 Feb – 22 Mar** — the
  second-largest fringe in the world breaks this on day one. Piccolo Spoleto
  (22 May – 7 Jun) and Perth (Jan–Feb) break it too. The axis has to become an
  arbitrary date range, which is a rewrite of the calendar rendering and the
  window maths, not a config swap.
- **The day axis is 09:00 → 27:00** (`plan/plan.js:70-71`), with a default day end
  of 25:00, because a Fringe evening runs past midnight and late shows fold onto
  the previous festival night. That is a real cultural property of *this*
  festival. A design-week or exhibition festival is a 10:00–18:00 opening-hours
  model with no after-midnight concept at all, and a Spanish-scheduled festival
  would push later still.
- **Every show has ticketed performances with start times.** Milan's Fuorisalone,
  the Edinburgh Art Festival and the Venice Biennale are *exhibitions* — open
  during hours, not at times. The scheduling engine has no concept of "drop in
  any time between 10:00 and 18:00, allow 45 minutes", and that is arguably the
  single largest missing capability for the non-theatre candidates.
- **Ticket-status vocabulary is Tikketr's enum.** `plan/lib/availability.js:22`
  denylists `SOLD_OUT`, `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` and friends — values from
  one ticketing platform. Another festival's platform has a different vocabulary,
  or none. The concept ("is this bookable") generalises; the strings do not.
- **The show ID is an edfringe slug.** It is the join key between favourites,
  the catalogue and deep links (`plan/lib/favourites.js:7,28`). Portability needs
  a `(festivalId, showId)` pair throughout, including in `localStorage` keys —
  otherwise a stored Edinburgh shortlist collides with an Adelaide one.

### Medium — tuned values presented as physics

- **Walking speed is Edinburgh's terrain.** `plan/lib/travel.js:18` dials walking
  down to ~3.33 km/h explicitly because of "Edinburgh's closes, hills, stairs and
  festival crowds", and `car: 22` km/h is calibrated to "the congested August city
  centre". Applied to flat, sprawling Adelaide these are simply wrong — and wrong
  in the direction that silently drops schedulable shows.
- **There is no public-transport mode.** `plan/lib/travel.js:12` offers walk/bike/
  car only, with the stated reason that honest headway-aware bus times aren't
  available. That is defensible in a compact walkable centre. In Adelaide (562
  venues), Melbourne or Montreal, transit *is* the mode, and its absence is a
  correctness problem rather than a missing nicety.
- **Crow-flies distance stands in for routing.** Fine across Edinburgh's Old Town;
  much worse across a river, a rail corridor or Venice's canals.
- **Geography defaults.** `js/app.js:20` defaults to central Edinburgh;
  `js/places.js:17,30` bounds the Nominatim geocoder to a greater-Edinburgh box
  and `inEdinburgh()` gates results by it; `shared/geo.js:12` deliberately ignores
  a real user location that is nowhere near Edinburgh. All three are correct today
  and all three actively break elsewhere.

### Easy — one-line config once a descriptor exists

- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:141` — `TZID = "Europe/London"` (but see the DST note in §4d).
- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:197` — ICS UIDs suffixed `@edfringenow.com`.
- `plan/lib/hydrate.js:13` — `IMAGE_HOST_PREFIX` pinned to `registration.edfringe.com`.
- `js/app.js:2544` — `en-GB` date formatting.
- `plan/index.html:298`, `plan/plan.js:1588`, `plan/lib/search.js:12,50` — `£`.
- `shared/affiliates.js:75` — Booking.com search hard-coded to `ss: "Edinburgh"`,
  and the Omio route pages likewise. Affiliate partners and their coverage differ
  by country, so this is easy to *parameterise* and separately a commercial
  question.

### Product-level, outside the code

- **The brand is the city.** "EdFringeNow", `edfringenow.com`, and the ICS UID
  domain all name one festival. A multi-festival product needs a different name,
  and that decision gates the domain and the deep-link contract.
- **"Two or three shows a day" and "don't fill the day"** are Fringe-culture
  advice this product's defaults encode. They may not be the right defaults for a
  design week or a jazz festival.

---

## 6. A plausible order of work

Sequenced so each step is useful on its own and none is wasted if the next is
never taken:

1. **Resolve the data-source question for Edinburgh itself** (Tier 1 official API
   vs. the current Tier 2 scrape, and whether committed static data is licence-
   compatible). This sets the pattern for everything after it.
2. **Make the calendar an arbitrary date range** instead of a fixed month. This is
   independently correct — the current data already spans 24 Jul – 31 Aug and the
   July previews fall off the axis — and it is the largest single blocker.
3. **Extract the festival descriptor** and route the constants in §5 through it,
   with Edinburgh as the only entry. No behaviour change; the diff is the point.
4. **Add an i18n layer and `Intl`-based formatting**, still English-only.
5. **Prove it with a second English festival** (Brighton or Perth) end to end,
   including the intake question — that is where the model gets tested, not the
   engine.
6. Only then consider a non-English festival, and only with the translation cost
   in §4b priced honestly.

---

## 7. What this sketch does not answer

- Whether any candidate festival has an accessible programme at all. Every
  feasibility claim above is conditional on a probe nobody has run.
- Whether the Edinburgh Festivals Listings API licence permits this repo's
  committed-static-data architecture. §2.2 raises it; it is unresolved.
- How exhibition-style events (open hours, no start times) would be modelled — the
  gap that rules out most of the non-theatre candidates as things stand.
- Whether a second festival is a second *market* or a second *product*. If the
  audiences don't overlap, most of the leverage assumed here doesn't exist.
- Anything about cost, demand or commercial viability. This is a technical sketch
  only.

+  (22 May – 7 Jun) and Perth (Jan–Feb) break it too. The axis has to become an
+  arbitrary date range, which is a rewrite of the calendar rendering and the
+  window maths, not a config swap.
+- **The day axis is 09:00 → 27:00** (`plan/plan.js:70-71`), with a default day end
+  of 25:00, because a Fringe evening runs past midnight and late shows fold onto
+  the previous festival night. That is a real cultural property of *this*
+  festival. A design-week or exhibition festival is a 10:00–18:00 opening-hours
+  model with no after-midnight concept at all, and a Spanish-scheduled festival
+  would push later still.
+- **Every show has ticketed performances with start times.** Milan's Fuorisalone,
+  the Edinburgh Art Festival and the Venice Biennale are *exhibitions* — open
+  during hours, not at times. The scheduling engine has no concept of "drop in
+  any time between 10:00 and 18:00, allow 45 minutes", and that is arguably the
+  single largest missing capability for the non-theatre candidates.
+- **Ticket-status vocabulary is Tikketr's enum.** `plan/lib/availability.js:22`
+  denylists `SOLD_OUT`, `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` and friends — values from
+  one ticketing platform. Another festival's platform has a different vocabulary,
+  or none. The concept ("is this bookable") generalises; the strings do not.
+- **The show ID is an edfringe slug.** It is the join key between favourites,
+  the catalogue and deep links (`plan/lib/favourites.js:7,28`). Portability needs
+  a `(festivalId, showId)` pair throughout, including in `localStorage` keys —
+  otherwise a stored Edinburgh shortlist collides with an Adelaide one.
+
+### Medium — tuned values presented as physics
+
+- **Walking speed is Edinburgh's terrain.** `plan/lib/travel.js:18` dials walking
+  down to ~3.33 km/h explicitly because of "Edinburgh's closes, hills, stairs and
+  festival crowds", and `car: 22` km/h is calibrated to "the congested August city
+  centre". Applied to flat, sprawling Adelaide these are simply wrong — and wrong
+  in the direction that silently drops schedulable shows.
+- **There is no public-transport mode.** `plan/lib/travel.js:12` offers walk/bike/
+  car only, with the stated reason that honest headway-aware bus times aren't
+  available. That is defensible in a compact walkable centre. In Adelaide (562
+  venues), Melbourne or Montreal, transit *is* the mode, and its absence is a
+  correctness problem rather than a missing nicety.
+- **Crow-flies distance stands in for routing.** Fine across Edinburgh's Old Town;
+  much worse across a river, a rail corridor or Venice's canals.
+- **Geography defaults.** `js/app.js:20` defaults to central Edinburgh;
+  `js/places.js:17,30` bounds the Nominatim geocoder to a greater-Edinburgh box
+  and `inEdinburgh()` gates results by it; `shared/geo.js:12` deliberately ignores
+  a real user location that is nowhere near Edinburgh. All three are correct today
+  and all three actively break elsewhere.
+
+### Easy — one-line config once a descriptor exists
+
+- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:141` — `TZID = "Europe/London"` (but see the DST note in §4d).
+- `plan/lib/itinerary.js:197` — ICS UIDs suffixed `@edfringenow.com`.
+- `plan/lib/hydrate.js:13` — `IMAGE_HOST_PREFIX` pinned to `registration.edfringe.com`.
+- `js/app.js:2544` — `en-GB` date formatting.
+- `plan/index.html:298`, `plan/plan.js:1588`, `plan/lib/search.js:12,50` — `£`.
+- `shared/affiliates.js:75` — Booking.com search hard-coded to `ss: "Edinburgh"`,
+  and the Omio route pages likewise. Affiliate partners and their coverage differ
+  by country, so this is easy to *parameterise* and separately a commercial
+  question.
+
+### Product-level, outside the code
+
+- **The brand is the city.** "EdFringeNow", `edfringenow.com`, and the ICS UID
+  domain all name one festival. A multi-festival product needs a different name,
+  and that decision gates the domain and the deep-link contract.
+- **"Two or three shows a day" and "don't fill the day"** are Fringe-culture
+  advice this product's defaults encode. They may not be the right defaults for a
+  design week or a jazz festival.
+
+---
+
+## 6. A plausible order of work
+
+Sequenced so each step is useful on its own and none is wasted if the next is
+never taken:
+
+1. **Resolve the data-source question for Edinburgh itself** (Tier 1 official API
+   vs. the current Tier 2 scrape, and whether committed static data is licence-
+   compatible). This sets the pattern for everything after it.
+2. **Make the calendar an arbitrary date range** instead of a fixed month. This is
+   independently correct — the current data already spans 24 Jul – 31 Aug and the
+   July previews fall off the axis — and it is the largest single blocker.
+3. **Extract the festival descriptor** and route the constants in §5 through it,
+   with Edinburgh as the only entry. No behaviour change; the diff is the point.
+4. **Add an i18n layer and `Intl`-based formatting**, still English-only.
+5. **Prove it with a second English festival** (Brighton or Perth) end to end,
+   including the intake question — that is where the model gets tested, not the
+   engine.
+6. Only then consider a non-English festival, and only with the translation cost
+   in §4b priced honestly.
+
+---
+
+## 7. What this sketch does not answer
+
+- Whether any candidate festival has an accessible programme at all. Every
+  feasibility claim above is conditional on a probe nobody has run.
+- Whether the Edinburgh Festivals Listings API licence permits this repo's
+  committed-static-data architecture. §2.2 raises it; it is unresolved.
+- How exhibition-style events (open hours, no start times) would be modelled — the
+  gap that rules out most of the non-theatre candidates as things stand.
+- Whether a second festival is a second *market* or a second *product*. If the
+  audiences don't overlap, most of the leverage assumed here doesn't exist.
+- Anything about cost, demand or commercial viability. This is a technical sketch
+  only.

1	# Taking the planner to other festivals — a first design sketch
2	
3	> **Status: rudimentary.** This is a sketch, not a plan of record. Nothing here
4	> is committed to, no code change is proposed yet, and several sections end in a
5	> question rather than an answer. Its job is to make the shape of the problem
6	> visible — and in particular to surface the Edinburgh assumptions that are
7	> currently invisible because they are spelled as constants, comments and
8	> regexes rather than as configuration.
9	>
10	> Scope: the **planner** (`/plan`) primarily, since that is where the model
11	> lives; the Now page is noted where it differs.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. What the planning model actually is
16	
17	Stripped of Edinburgh, the planner is four pure computations over a catalogue of
18	`{show → performances[]}` with venue coordinates:
19	
20	| Step | Module | Depends on |
21	|---|---|---|
22	| favourites text → show IDs | `plan/lib/favourites.js` | a stable show ID and a canonical show URL |
23	| performances → *available* performances | `plan/lib/availability.js` | a ticket-status vocabulary |
24	| venue pair → travel minutes | `plan/lib/travel.js` | coordinates + a speed model |
25	| available performances → clash-free itinerary | `plan/lib/engine.js` | a day window, meal bands, per-day caps |
26	| itinerary → CSV / ICS | `plan/lib/itinerary.js` | a timezone and a wall-clock convention |
27	
28	**None of that is Edinburgh-specific in principle.** "Given a set of things I
29	want to see, each with several showings across a date range, in venues that take
30	time to travel between — which can I actually fit?" is a general problem. The
31	earliest-finish-first greedy in `engine.js` does not know what a Fringe is.
32	
33	What *is* Edinburgh-specific is everything around it: where the catalogue comes
34	from, what its ticket statuses are called, what a date window looks like, what
35	currency and language it is in, and how a user's shortlist gets into the tool.
36	Those are the four sections below.
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 2. Data accessibility — the binding constraint
41	
42	This decides feasibility, and it is worse than the language problem.
43	
44	### 2.1 The tiers
45	
46	Any candidate festival falls into one of four tiers, and the tier — not the
47	festival's size — determines the cost:
48	
49	- **Tier 1 — official, licensed API.** A documented feed with an access key.
50	  Cheap, legally clean, and stable across years.
51	- **Tier 2 — an undocumented but stable web API.** What edfringe.com actually
52	  is today: a Next.js SPA over a Tikketr GraphQL endpoint, reachable with public
53	  anonymous credentials (see [`scraper/SCRAPING.md`](../scraper/SCRAPING.md)).
54	  Workable, but it breaks without notice and carries no licence.
55	- **Tier 3 — HTML scraping only.** Per-festival parsers, brittle against every
56	  site redesign, and a per-festival maintenance burden that compounds.
57	- **Tier 4 — no machine-readable programme.** A PDF brochure and a paper guide.
58	  Not viable.
59	
60	### 2.2 What we know today
61	
62	Edinburgh is unusually well served, and this is easy to mistake for normal:
63	
64	- **Tier 2 is already built** — the Tikketr GraphQL scrape in `scraper/`.
65	- **Tier 1 exists and is not currently used.** The
66	  [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)
67	  is a free API over the official listings database for *all eleven* Edinburgh
68	  festivals (640,000+ performances), with `events` and `venues` endpoints and a
69	  self-service access key.
70	
71	That second point deserves a decision of its own, because whichever source is
72	chosen becomes the template every other city is fitted to. Its terms are not
73	free of consequences for this repo's architecture:
74	
75	- Fringe listings require **separate approval from a Fringe review team**;
76	  development happens against a demonstration dataset first.
77	- Applications must **refresh at least every 24 hours**, and must **not
78	  redistribute the data as a static dump to third parties**.
79	- Show links must **deep-link to edfringe.com**, and the app must state it is not
80	  official.
81	
82	This repo currently commits generated `data/` files to git and serves them from
83	GitHub Pages — which is, read strictly, a static dump published to the world on
84	a scrape cadence rather than a 24-hour client refresh. Whether that is compatible
85	with the licence is an open legal/architectural question, and it is a *prerequisite*
86	for the multi-festival work rather than a detail of it, because the answer
87	("client fetches a live feed" vs. "we ship a snapshot") changes the whole data
88	layer.
89	
90	For every other candidate city, no equivalent Tier 1 source has been found.
91	Assume Tier 2 or Tier 3 per festival until a probe says otherwise.
92	
93	### 2.3 The favourites-import problem is per-festival
94	
95	The planner's front door — a shortlist you already built elsewhere — is the least
96	portable part of the product. Today it depends on:
97	
98	- `plan/lib/favourites.js:7` — a regex hard-coded to
99	  `edfringe.com/tickets/whats-on/<slug>`;
100	- the fact that edfringe.com has favouriting at all;
101	- a **third-party Chrome extension** to get that list out as CSV, since no native
102	  export is documented.
103	
104	That chain has to be re-established, festival by festival, and there is no reason
105	to expect it exists. A portable product probably cannot depend on it: the
106	in-tool search path (`plan/lib/search.js`, already built) is the one intake that
107	travels, and for a new festival it may have to be the *only* one.
108	
109	---
110	
111	## 3. Integration — what the code would need
112	
113	### 3.1 A festival descriptor
114	
115	The natural shape is one **festival adapter** plus one **festival descriptor**,
116	with the pure engine untouched. The descriptor is the config object that every
117	constant listed in §5 currently stands in for:
118	
119	```
120	{
121	  id, name,
122	  city, country,
123	  locale, timezone, currency,
124	  runStart, runEnd,              // real dates, not "August 1–31"
125	  siteBase, showUrlPattern,      // deep-link contract
126	  imageHostPrefix,
127	  ticketStatus: { unavailable[], nonTicketed[] },
128	  genres[], subgenres[],         // per-festival taxonomy, not a shared enum
129	  travel: { modes[], speedsKmh{} },
130	  defaultCentre: [lat, lng],
131	  geocodeBounds,
132	}
133	```
134	
135	Two design calls worth making early, because they are hard to reverse:
136	
137	- **One descriptor per *festival*, not per *city*.** Edinburgh in August is six
138	  festivals with different date ranges and different data sources. If the unit is
139	  a city, the Adelaide/Avignon cases fit but Edinburgh itself does not.
140	- **Taxonomies are per-festival data, not a shared enum.** edfringe's 10 genres
141	  and 104 subgenres are its own vocabulary. Mapping Avignon's *théâtre / humour /
142	  cirque* split onto it would be a lossy translation nobody asked for. A shared
143	  cross-festival taxonomy is a much later problem, and probably not worth it.
144	
145	### 3.2 The adapter boundary
146	
147	`scraper/` becomes per-festival fetchers behind one normalizer contract, rather
148	than one script that knows edfringe's schema. The contract is already implicitly
149	defined — `data/normalized/shows.json`'s shape, decoded by `js/app.js`'s
150	`adaptShow` and `plan/lib/hydrate.js`'s `rehydrateShows` — but it is not written
151	down anywhere as a spec, and it uses **positional index encoding** against
152	`data/venues.json`'s global lookup lists. Any second festival forces that
153	implicit contract to become explicit, and the positional encoding to become
154	per-festival rather than global.
155	
156	### 3.3 Data layout and payload
157	
158	Today the planner fetches the full `data/normalized/shows.json` (~1.1 MB gzipped,
159	4,078 shows) on load. That is already noted as borderline in
160	[`plan/README.md`](../plan/README.md). Multi-festival makes it a real constraint,
161	and the fix is structural rather than an optimisation: data is partitioned per

gitDiff.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,249 @@
+# Festival cities beyond Edinburgh
+
+Which other cities in the world carry the Edinburgh-in-August pattern — many
+overlapping festivals, thousands of temporary show runs and exhibitions, and a
+city swarming with visitors who have to *choose*. This page exists because the
+product's premise (overwhelm + reachability) is a property of that pattern, not
+of Edinburgh, so anywhere the pattern recurs is a candidate market. It ranks
+candidates by how close they are **structurally** (does the same mechanism
+produce the overwhelm?) rather than by fame. Compiled once, refined in place.
+
+## Key insights
+
+- Adelaide is the only real peer, and still less than half of Edinburgh: 1,648 shows to 3,649.
+- Avignon OFF is the closest structural twin — 1,780 open-access shows in 141 theatres inside one walled town.
+- 300+ fringes exist worldwide, but only three sell more than 250,000 tickets.
+- Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API. No other festival city found has an equivalent.

+  months-long run means opening hours, not performance times.
+- **Kassel — Documenta** (every five years, 100 days) and the roving **Manifesta**
+  are the same category, unassessed.

+- **Nothing is close on density.** Edinburgh's Fringe alone is ~2.2× Adelaide on
+  show count (3,649 vs 1,648, both 2026) and ~2.4× on tickets (2.6m in 2025 vs
+  1.08m in 2026 — the newest full-year figure each publishes), in a smaller, more
+  walkable centre, and it overlaps five other major festivals. The overwhelm the
+  product exists to solve is genuinely worst here.
+- **Edinburgh is the only candidate with an official aggregation layer.** The
+  Edinburgh Festivals Listings API is a free API over the official listings
+  database for all **11** Edinburgh festivals, carrying over **640,000
+  performances**, with `events` and `venues` endpoints, a self-service access key,
+  and a licence permitting commercial use. Fringe listings need separate approval
+  from a Fringe review team, applications must refresh at least every 24 hours and
+  must deep-link to edfringe.com. No equivalent single-source feed was found for

+  nothing. That asymmetry, not language, is the real cost of a second city.

input.body:
Closes #198.

Two documents, no code changes.

## 1. `product-wiki/festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/` — a new wiki page

Which other cities carry the Edinburgh-in-August pattern, ranked by how close they are **structurally** (does the same mechanism produce the overwhelm?) rather than by fame.

- **Four mechanisms** that produce an Edinburgh-shaped city, separated because each implies a different data and product problem: open access; a curated core with an unofficial "off"; a festival *season*; and long exhibition runs (which make a city swarm without producing any scheduling problem).
- **The two close analogues** with 2026 figures — **Adelaide** (1,648 shows / 562 venues / ~1.08m tickets, and *not* one calendar month: 20 Feb – 22 Mar) and **Avignon OFF** (1,780 shows / 141 theatres / ~27,000 performances, 54% average fill).
- **An "Other potential candidate events" section**, grouped by mechanism: Perth, Brighton, Makhanda, Toronto and the fringe tail; Milan's Fuorisalone, Piccolo Spoleto, Miami Beach, Cannes, SXSW; Montreal, Sibiu, Galway, Salzburg; Venice, Documenta, Manifesta.
- **Where Edinburgh is still singular**, including the load-bearing finding: Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API covering all 11 of its festivals (640k+ performances), and **no candidate city has an equivalent**. Data accessibility, not language, is the binding constraint on a second city.
- Salzburg is kept in deliberately as the boundary case — 208 curated performances is a crowded city with no overwhelm problem, which is the distinction the page is drawing.

Every claim is cited (29 sources). Per-candidate data accessibility is recorded as the top open question, since no probe has been run.

`product-wiki/README.md` gains the index entry.

## 2. `docs/multi-festival-design.md` — a rudimentary design sketch

Explicitly labelled a sketch, not a plan of record. Its job is to make the Edinburgh assumptions visible, since they are currently spelled as constants, comments and regexes rather than as configuration.

- **Data accessibility** — a four-tier model, and the observation that this repo already sits on Tier 2 (the Tikketr GraphQL scrape) while an unused Tier 1 source exists. Flags an unresolved question worth answering *before* any global work: the official API's licence forbids redistributing data as a static dump and requires ≥24h refresh, which sits awkwardly with committing generated `data/` and serving it from GitHub Pages. Also notes that the favourites-import front door is the least portable part of the product.
- **Integration** — a festival descriptor plus per-festival adapters behind one normalizer contract, with `plan/lib/engine.js` untouched; two calls made early because they're hard to reverse (descriptor per *festival* not per *city*; taxonomies are per-festival data, not a shared enum).
- **Localization** — four separable problems usually conflated: UI strings (no i18n layer exists), content strings (Avignon is ~90% French companies; a localized UI over French content is the realistic target), formatting/units, and timezone. Notes that Adelaide's run crosses a DST transition.
- **Edinburgh-specific assumptions**, graded hard/medium/easy, with verified `file:line` references. The largest: the calendar axis is one calendar month (`plan/plan.js:56-59`), which the world's second-largest fringe breaks on day one; the 09:00→27:00 day axis; the Tikketr status vocabulary; Edinburgh-tuned walking and driving speeds presented as physics; no transit mode; and no model at all for exhibition-style open-hours events.
- A staged order of work, sequenced so each step is useful alone, and a closing list of what the sketch does *not* answer.

## Verification

`npm run verify` green (tests, JS/Python syntax, normalizer self-test). Both Claudinite runners green — and the wiki checks were proven live with a see-it-fail (renaming `## Open questions` produced the expected blocking `product-wiki-page-sections` finding, then reverted).

Nothing under `product-wiki/product-requirements/` was touched, and the design doc makes no reference to `product-wiki/`, so the isolation wall holds.

Both landed — [PR #199](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/199), closing [#198](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/198).

**The wiki page** (`product-wiki/festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/`) turns the chat answer into a cited page organised by *mechanism* rather than by fame — open access, curated-core-plus-off, festival season, long exhibition run — because each implies a different data and product problem. Research firmed up the numbers I'd given you from memory: Avignon OFF is larger than I said (1,780 shows in 141 theatres, not ~1,500), and Adelaide 2026 is 1,648 shows / 562 venues / ~1.08m tickets. The "Other potential candidate events" section is there as asked, grouped the same way.

The finding that reframes the whole thing: **Edinburgh is the only candidate city with an official cross-festival listings API** — a free, licensed feed over all 11 festivals with 640k+ performances, which this repo isn't currently using. No equivalent exists for Adelaide, Avignon, Perth, Milan or Montreal. So the constraint on a second city is data accessibility, not translation.

**The design doc** (`docs/multi-festival-design.md`) covers your four axes, and section 5 is the "aspects you didn't consider" list, graded and line-referenced. The ones I'd flag:

- **The calendar axis is a single calendar month** (`plan/plan.js:56-59`, `MONTH = "08"`, days 1–31). Adelaide runs 20 Feb – 22 Mar — the world's second-largest fringe breaks it immediately. That's a rewrite of the calendar and window maths, not a config swap, and it's independently worth doing since the July previews already fall off the axis.
- **Nothing models exhibition-style events** — open 10:00–18:00, drop in any time. That's most of the non-theatre candidates (Fuorisalone, Venice, even Edinburgh's own Art Festival) ruled out as things stand.
- **Travel speeds are Edinburgh's terrain presented as physics** — walking dialled to 3.33 km/h for closes and hills, car at 22 km/h for the congested August centre — and there's no transit mode. In Adelaide's 562 venues that's a correctness problem, not a missing nicety.
- **A licence question that gates everything else**: the official API forbids redistributing data as a static dump and wants ≥24h refresh, which sits awkwardly with committing `data/` and serving it from GitHub Pages. Worth resolving for Edinburgh first, since whichever source wins becomes the template every other city gets fitted to.

Verification: `npm run verify` green, both Claudinite runners green, and I proved the wiki checks were actually firing with a see-it-fail rather than trusting a silent pass.

Want me to watch the PR for CI failures and review comments?

> ✅ Both deliverables are written, verified, committed, pushed and open for review. Nothing outstanding on my side.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/EdFringeNow/.claude/skills/merge-to-main

The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

## 1. `product-wiki/festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/` — a new wiki page

Which other cities carry the Edinburgh-in-August pattern, ranked by how close they are **structurally** (does the same mechanism produce the overwhelm?) rather than by fame.

- **Four mechanisms** that produce an Edinburgh-shaped city, separated because each implies a different data and product problem: open access; a curated core with an unofficial "off"; a festival *season*; and long exhibition runs (which make a city swarm without producing any scheduling problem).
- **The two close analogues** with 2026 figures — **Adelaide** (1,648 shows / 562 venues / ~1.08m tickets, and *not* one calendar month: 20 Feb – 22 Mar) and **Avignon OFF** (1,780 shows / 141 theatres / ~27,000 performances, 54% average fill).

- **Where Edinburgh is still singular**, including the load-bearing finding: Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API covering all 11 of its festivals (640k+ performances), and **no candidate city has an equivalent**. Data accessibility, not language, is the binding constraint on a second city.
- Salzburg is kept in deliberately as the boundary case — 208 curated performances is a crowded city with no overwhelm problem, which is the distinction the page is drawing.

Every claim is cited (29 sources). Per-candidate data accessibility is recorded as the top open question, since no probe has been run.

- A staged order of work, sequenced so each step is useful alone, and a closing list of what the sketch does *not* answer.

    independent Fringe Society charity's box office; edfest.com is the seven
    big operators' own storefront. The >=25% allocation model explains the
    NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE status. Operator census from our own
    catalogue: 24 families cover 83% of 4,100 shows, tail of 171 venues. No
    affiliate/agent/API selling route exists anywhere. The scrape has no full

1	# Market & audience
2	
3	The scale of the Edinburgh Fringe and the audience behaviour EdFringeNow is built
4	for. Two decisions live here, not one: the in-the-moment "what can I make right
5	now" (the home site, *Fringe Discover*) and the weeks-earlier "which shows, which
6	dates" (the planner at `/plan`). Compiled once, refined in place.
7	
8	## Key insights
9	
10	- 3,649 Fringe shows across 258 venues in 2026 — plus ~900 more events from seven other August festivals.
11	- 37% of people struggle to pick a show. Two thirds buy just one ticket.
12	- 78% come to see something they would not normally — they want surprise, not better filters.
13	- A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh. Two thirds travel in and plan months ahead.
14	- The advice everyone gives is: do not fill the day. Two or three shows.
15	- Beds may pick the dates, not shows — over half cannot find an affordable room nearby.
16	- Nobody has data on how people choose in the street. Not us, not anyone.
17	
18	## Scale
19	
20	### 2026 festival (running 7–31 August 2026)
21	
22	- **3,649 shows** across **258 venues**, **53,884 performances**, artists from
23	  **71 countries** — announced at the programme launch on 4 June 2026.
24	- Genre split at launch: **1,401 comedy**, **1,025 theatre**, **168 musicals and
25	  opera**.
26	- Smaller than 2025 on both counts (3,893 shows / 301 venues), and still two
27	  orders of magnitude more than any one visitor can see.
28	
29	### 2025 festival (latest full ticket data)
30	
31	- **3,893 shows** across **301 venues**, **53,942 performances**, artists from
32	  **62 countries**.
33	- **~2.6 million tickets** issued (2,604,404) — roughly flat on 2024, still below
34	  the 2019 pre-pandemic peak of about 3 million.
35	- **edfringe.com took over 3 million visits and 37 million page views**, and
36	  ~4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to the site to help audiences choose.
37	
38	*(2025's ticket figures stay on this page because they remain the newest
39	issued-ticket data — the Fringe Society publishes each year's ticket and audience
40	data after the festival closes, so 2026's cannot land before late August 2026.)*
41	
42	This scale is the product premise: the official programme is a catalogue that
43	rewards planning ahead and overwhelms the person deciding in the moment.
44	
45	### The Fringe is not all of August
46	
47	The page's scale figures — and the product built on them — cover one festival.
48	Seven others run concurrently: the International Festival (147 performances),
49	the Military Tattoo (nightly), the Deaf Festival (80+ events), the Film Festival
50	(38 features), the Art Festival (40+ mostly-free exhibitions), the Book Festival
51	(~600 events) and Fringe by the Sea. Roughly 900 further events, overlapping the
52	Fringe almost completely in time and largely in place.
53	
54	That changes the overwhelm problem's shape rather than only its size. The Fringe
55	is ~80% of August's events, so any relevance- or proximity-ranked list shows a
56	Fringe-only city; and the non-Fringe events are the *scarcer* ones — a Fringe
57	show plays ~25 times, a Book Festival author appears once. The programme's scale
58	buries exactly what cannot be seen twice. Dates, counts, locations, the six
59	different shapes an "event" takes across these festivals, and whether the data is
60	obtainable are all worked through on
61	[festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md).
62	
63	## The overwhelm / decision problem
64	
65	Fringe Society audience data puts numbers on it:
66	
67	- **37% of audiences struggled to pick a show** to go and see.
68	- **Two thirds of ticket buyers bought only one ticket** — for most of the
69	  audience the Fringe is a single decision, not a curated run of shows.
70	- **78% came to the Fringe to see something they wouldn't go and see otherwise** —
71	  the appetite is for discovery, not for a known quantity.
72	
73	The standard advice around that, consistent across guides and relevant to both
74	surfaces:
75	
76	- With more than 3,800 shows, choosing "can feel like a daunting task"; the
77	  advice is to lean on filters, star ratings and reviews, and to **embrace
78	  serendipity** — the show you'd never have booked is often the one people still
79	  talk about.
80	- **Leave travel time.** Edinburgh is compact but August streets are not; guides
81	  repeat that venues which look close together are not close in August — the
82	  reachability constraint Fringe Discover makes first-class rather than an
83	  afterthought.
84	- **Two to three shows a day** is the pace commonly advised as comfortable —
85	  leaving room to eat, walk, and stand still.
86	- **Don't fill the day.** Fringe CEO Tony Lankester's "rule of thirds" — about a
87	  third of the time pre-planned, the rest left open — alongside reporting that
88	  visitors who combined structured planning with open time were more satisfied
89	  than those who over-scheduled.
90	
91	That last point is load-bearing here: the gaps a planner deliberately leaves are
92	exactly the gaps the live surface exists to fill.
93	
94	## Two crowds, not one
95	
96	This page previously described a single audience (the in-the-moment one) because
97	it was seeded from the *Fringe Discover* brief. The repo now ships two front
98	ends — the mobile-first home site and the desktop-first planner at `/plan` — and
99	they serve different people, or the same people in different states.
100	
101	### A. Live, in-festival — "what can I make right now"
102	
103	- **On the ground, deciding for the next hour or two.** Location, travel mode and
104	  the next commitment are the constraints; the catalogue is noise.
105	- **A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh** — locals have no trip to plan and
106	  no accommodation to book, and decide close to the moment by construction.
107	- **Same-day supply is a real channel, and an in-person one.** The Half Price Hut
108	  sells same-day (and next-morning) tickets from the Fringe Box Office only — not
109	  online, not in the app — opening 12 August in 2026, 10:00–18:00 daily.
110	- **Walk-up availability is not constant across the run.** Guides report walk-ups
111	  are easy in the opening week and that by weeks two and three popular shows —
112	  comedy headliners especially — sell out days in advance. The live surface's
113	  usefulness therefore moves with the calendar as well as the hour.
114	- **How the decision is actually made in the street is undocumented.** Posters,
115	  Royal Mile flyering, star ratings and word of mouth clearly drive a large share
116	  of it, but practitioners writing about Fringe marketing state plainly that
117	  nobody knows what works — there is no measured breakdown of in-the-moment
118	  discovery channels to cite.
119	
120	### B. Trip planners optimising around favourite shows
121	
122	- **Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh** — they choose dates,
123	  book beds and travel, and assemble a show list long before August.
124	- **Audiences now engage months ahead.** Reporting on how the Fringe audience has
125	  changed describes a 2026 audience that follows artists online, votes in polls
126	  and treats the festival as a live-entertainment marketplace well before August —
127	  a marked shift from the "turn up and grab a flyer" Fringe of a decade ago.
128	- **Accommodation binds *which dates* a trip can happen**, not as a footnote:
129	  coverage of the festival's accommodation crisis reports over half of people
130	  hoping to attend could not find an affordable place to stay within a 90-minute
131	  commute. Dates get chosen against beds as much as against shows — something the
132	  planner's "pick my best dates" currently ignores.
133	- **The favourites list is the planner's raw material, and it lives elsewhere.**
134	  Shows are favourited on edfringe.com and saved in the official app's *My
135	  Planner* (which syncs to a personal calendar). Getting that list *out* as a CSV
136	  is served by a third-party Chrome extension ("EdFringe Favourites to CSV",
137	  updated per festival year); no native edfringe.com CSV export is documented.

... [109 lines truncated] ...

31	"Can I get a ticket" comes from the per-performance `ticketStatus`, not the
32	`soldOut` flag: a performance can be `soldOut: false` and still have nothing to
33	sell online (`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE`). The site treats `SOLD_OUT` and
34	`NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` as unavailable and everything else as available
35	(`NO_TICKETS_STATUSES` in `js/app.js`), and unknown means available. Any new
36	availability logic — client or scraper — keys off `ticketStatus`; `soldOut` is
37	carried through for display only.
38	
39	## Prices are fetched once, and "unknown" is a third state the encoding must keep
40	
41	`data/prices.json` is a fetch-once cache (`scraper/fetch_prices.py`), off the
42	nightly path: a show's price bands are set when it goes on sale, unlike its
43	ticket status. `refresh-shows` reads the cache and carries the amounts through
44	untouched — it never re-fetches them. So the festival keeps adding shows the
45	cache has never seen, and **a show with no price is a normal, permanent state of
46	the data**, not a gap the pipeline should close.
47	
48	Which means the encoding carries three states, not two, and every stage has to
49	preserve the distinction:
50	
51	| state | master | wire |
52	|---|---|---|
53	| costs nothing | `priceMin: 0` | `pm: 0` |
54	| priced | `priceMin: 22.5` | `pm: 22.5` |
55	| unknown | `priceMin: null` | no `pm` key at all |
56	
57	`priceMin: 0` and `free: true` are **not** the same claim and don't always agree.
58	The flag comes from the listing; the £0 can also come from the price API, which
59	returns a single `Price band 1` at £0.00 for a handful of shows the listing
60	doesn't flag free — pay-what-you-want, or a box office that never set a price
61	(10 of 3,664 in the first full run). Both readings are honest about what a ticket
62	costs, so the price path keys off `priceMin`, and `free` stays what the *listing*
63	said. Don't "fix" one to match the other.
64	
65	Never encode unknown as `0`, and never let a decoder default it to one: a stage
66	that collapses three states into two is lying about money, and nothing
67	downstream can recover the difference. What the site then *does* with an unknown
68	price is a product decision, not a pipeline one — it lives in `shared/price.js`.
69	
70	Two traps in the raw price payload, both already handled and both worth not
71	re-introducing: amounts arrive as **strings**, and nearly every show carries a
72	£0.00 "Personal Assistant" concession (a carer's companion ticket) that must not
73	be read as the cheapest price. See the pricing section of
74	[scraper/SCRAPING.md](../../../../scraper/SCRAPING.md).
75	
76	## The committed data is generated output — regenerate it, never hand-edit it
77	
78	`data/raw_pages/` is a git-ignored regenerable cache. `data/normalized/`,
79	`data/venues.json` and `data/days/` **are** committed, because the browser
80	fetches them — but they are still generator output. Fix the data by fixing
81	`scraper/normalize.py` and re-running it (`--merge` for a top-up, no flag for a
82	full rebuild from the raw cache); a hand-edit is silently overwritten by the next
83	`refresh-shows` run and leaves the bug in the generator.
84	
85	`data/prices.json` is the one exception, and it is an exception to the *direction*
86	rather than the rule: it is committed, but it is normalize.py's **input**, written
87	by `scraper/fetch_prices.py`. Nothing regenerates it on a schedule, so nothing
88	overwrites a hand-edit either — which is precisely why editing it by hand is still
89	wrong: the edit survives, silently disagreeing with the box office forever. Re-run
90	the fetch. The `edfringe-data-dir-is-generator-output` check allows it **by name**,
91	so a second file can't ride in on its shape.
92	
93	## Changing the wire format is a four-file change
94	
95	The day files and `shows.min.json` reference `data/venues.json`'s global lists
96	**by position** (`genre`, `room`, `subs`, `ts`; `g`, `rm`, `sg`, `ar`, `p[].t`).
97	That encoding has one producer and two decoders, and they must move together:
98	
99	- producer — `scraper/normalize.py` (`build_lookups` / `build_day_files` /
100	  `minify_master`)
...
57	- decoder 2 — `plan/lib/hydrate.js` `rehydrateShows`, the exact inverse of
58	  `minify_master`, round-tripped against the real committed files by
59	  `plan/lib/__tests__/hydrate.test.mjs`
60	
61	Add or drop an indexed field and all three change in the same commit. That the
62	indices still *resolve* is enforced by the `edfringe-lookup-indices` check — it
63	catches a lookup list regenerated without its day files, but nothing can catch a
64	decoder left reading the old key, so check both decoders by hand.
65	
66	The same three-way move applies to plain (non-indexed) wire keys such as the
67	price fields `pm` / `px`, with one extra hazard: the round-trip test compares the
68	rehydrated record to the master **as JSON**, so a new master key has to appear in
69	the *same position* in `normalize_event`'s dict and in `rehydrateShows`'s object
70	literal. Adding it in one place and appending it in the other fails the
71	round-trip on key order alone, which reads as a data bug and isn't one.

# product-wiki

Agent-maintained market, user, and competitor research for EdFringeNow, kept as
self-growing wikis under this directory (compile findings once, refine in place,
cite everything). This tree is **walled off from the app code** — nothing in the
repo may reference `product-wiki/` except the reviewed distillation under

# Beyond the Fringe — a multi-festival design proposal

> **Status:** proposal. No code changes accompany this document. It is written to
> be argued with, cut down, or rejected in parts — the phasing at the end assumes
> that.

## 1. The premise

The product is built on one festival. The city runs at least eight in August, and
they overlap almost completely:

| Festival | Dates 2026 | Rough scale |
|---|---|---|
| Festival Fringe | 7–31 Aug | 3,649 shows / 53,884 performances / 258 venues |
| International Festival | 7–30 Aug | 147 performances |
| Military Tattoo | 7–29 Aug (not Sun) | one show, nightly, ~9,000 seats |
| Deaf Festival | 7–16 Aug | 80+ events |
| Film Festival | 13–19 Aug | 38 features, 21 world premieres |
| Art Festival | 14–30 Aug | 40+ exhibitions, mostly free |
| Book Festival | 15–30 Aug | ~600 events |
| Fringe by the Sea | 31 Jul–9 Aug | small Fringe, **in North Berwick** |

Plus a June–July season that finishes before the Fringe opens (Hidden Door, the
Meadows Festival, Jazz & Blues, the Multicultural Festival's Carnival, Folk &
Food).

Two numbers govern every design decision below:

- **The Fringe is ~80% of August's events.** Anything ranked purely on relevance
  or proximity shows a Fringe-only city. Volume alone will bury the other seven.
- **Scarcity runs the opposite way.** A Fringe show plays ~25 times. A Book
  Festival author appears once. An EIFF screening is often a single showing. The
  events hardest to replace are exactly the ones volume ranking hides.

That inversion — abundance and scarcity pointing in opposite directions — is the
design opportunity, not a complication to be smoothed over.
